blocks.content: Database Architecture walked through the internal layers a query passes through. ACID Properties looks at the actual guarantees that architecture, the write ahead log, the buffer pool, the transaction system, is genuinely built to provide, specifically for grouped operations called transactions.

ACID is an acronym for four separate guarantees, atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability, and each one solves a genuinely real problem that shows up the moment more than one thing needs to happen together, or more than one user touches the database at the same time.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438106001-75802991.png
1. The Four Letters, at a Glance
blocks.text: 1. The Four Letters, at a Glance

blocks.content: Atomicity means a transaction happens fully, or not at all, there is no in between state where only part of it took effect. Consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another valid state, never leaving it in a state that violates the rules you have defined.

Isolation means concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other view of the data, even when many transactions run at the same time. Durability means once a transaction is committed, it genuinely survives a crash, it does not silently disappear.

2. Atomicity, With a Concrete Example

Transferring money between two accounts genuinely requires two separate steps, debiting one account and crediting the other. If only the debit happened and the credit failed, money would simply vanish, a genuinely serious bug.

Atomicity guarantees both steps happen together, or neither does, never just one. If anything goes wrong partway through, the entire transaction rolls back, leaving both accounts exactly as they were before the transfer was attempted.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438106002-96726002.png
3. Consistency, With a Concrete Example

Suppose a genuine business rule states an account balance can never go negative. A transaction attempts to withdraw more money than the account actually holds, which would violate that rule if it were allowed to succeed.

Consistency guarantees the database rejects that transaction entirely, rather than allowing it to leave the account in an invalid, rule violating state. The database only ever moves from one valid state to another, never through an invalid one, even temporarily.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438106003-649866725.png

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Confusing the C in ACID, consistency of business rules within a single database, with the C in the separate CAP theorem, which refers to consistency across multiple machines. These are genuinely related but distinct ideas, covered as their own separate topic next.
4. Isolation, With a Concrete Example

Two transactions running at the same time, transaction A reading and updating a row, transaction B reading and updating that same row concurrently, could genuinely interfere with each other if the database did nothing to prevent it, one transaction seeing the other half finished, uncommitted work.

Isolation guarantees each transaction sees a consistent, coherent view of the data, not the other transaction partially completed changes. Different databases offer different strengths of isolation, a topic covered in real depth later in this course under Transactions and Concurrency.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438106003-827105931.png
5. Durability, With a Concrete Example

A transaction commits successfully, and the database acknowledges that success back to the application. Moments later, the server genuinely crashes, power failure, hardware fault, an unexpected restart, something that would normally risk losing recent changes.

Durability guarantees the committed change is still there once the database comes back up, precisely because of the write ahead log mechanism covered in the earlier Database Architecture topic, which allows recovery to replay any committed change that had not yet been fully applied to its final location on disk.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438106004-828868345.png

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Durability is not magic, it is a direct, practical result of the write ahead log mechanism covered in the previous topic. Understanding that mechanism is what makes durability feel less like a black box guarantee.
6. A Worked Transaction
Putting all four properties together, a real transaction moving money between two accounts shows exactly how they combine in practice.

Atomicity ensures both updates apply together. Consistency ensures neither account ends up in an invalid state, like a negative balance if that rule exists. Isolation ensures another concurrent transaction does not see account A debited but account B not yet credited. And durability ensures that once COMMIT succeeds, the change survives even a crash immediately afterward.

8. Genuinely Common Misunderstandings

A few real misunderstandings about ACID show up often. Assuming every database fully guarantees all four properties by default, when in reality some databases, and some specific configurations, relax certain guarantees deliberately in exchange for performance or scale.

Confusing consistency in ACID with the C in the CAP theorem, two genuinely related but distinct concepts, covered clearly as separate topics in this course. And wrapping unrelated operations into one large transaction unnecessarily, which can hurt performance and increase the chance of conflicts with other concurrent transactions.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438106004-376333507.png
9. Common Mistakes

["Assuming ACID guarantees are universal across all databases: some databases relax specific guarantees deliberately for performance, worth checking explicitly.","Treating a long running transaction as free: longer transactions hold resources longer, increasing the chance of conflicts with other concurrent work.","Forgetting to actually test rollback behavior: atomicity only matters if your application correctly handles a transaction that genuinely fails and rolls back."]
items: Assuming ACID guarantees are universal across all databases: some databases relax specific guarantees deliberately for performance, worth checking explicitly.
Treating a long running transaction as free: longer transactions hold resources longer, increasing the chance of conflicts with other concurrent work.
Forgetting to actually test rollback behavior: atomicity only matters if your application correctly handles a transaction that genuinely fails and rolls back.

blocks.content: 10. Key Takeaways
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438106241-139732444.png

["ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability, four separate but related transaction guarantees.","Atomicity guarantees a transaction happens fully or not at all, preventing a partially applied, broken state.","Consistency guarantees a transaction only moves the database between valid states, never through an invalid one.","Isolation guarantees concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other view of the data.","Durability guarantees a committed transaction genuinely survives a crash, thanks to the write ahead log mechanism.","Not every database or configuration guarantees all four properties fully, worth checking explicitly for a given system."]
items: ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability, four separate but related transaction guarantees.
Atomicity guarantees a transaction happens fully or not at all, preventing a partially applied, broken state.
Consistency guarantees a transaction only moves the database between valid states, never through an invalid one.
Isolation guarantees concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other view of the data.
Durability guarantees a committed transaction genuinely survives a crash, thanks to the write ahead log mechanism.
Not every database or configuration guarantees all four properties fully, worth checking explicitly for a given system.
